title: How should you prepare if your case interview is one week away?
description: Interview next week? A simple, realistic plan for 7 days of case interview prep, with what to do each week.
hook: With one week to go, spend day one learning how a case flows, days two to six doing one full case a day plus a ten-minute drill aimed at your weakest skill, and day seven reviewing your fixes, rehearsing two fit stories and resting. A week will not make you an expert, but it is enough to fix the two or three habits that cost most candidates the most points. Here is the plan day by day, with what to do in each session.
body:
In this guide

  • What one week can and cannot do
  • The plan at a glance
  • Day 1: learn the shape of a case
  • Days 2 to 6: one case and one drill a day
  • Focused sprints for your weakest skill
  • Fit stories in a week
  • Day 7: review, rehearse, rest
  • Mistakes in the final week
  • If you fall behind
  • Check yourself

What one week can and cannot do

Seven days is not long enough to see every case type or to master every skill, so do not try. It is long enough to learn the standard flow of a case, do five full cases, and fix your two biggest weaknesses. That is a real difference: a candidate with a clear opening, a tailored structure and an answer-first close stands out even if their maths is merely solid.

The rule for the week: prioritise, don't cover. Every session should target something you have seen go wrong in your own practice.

The plan at a glance

DayMain taskTime
1Course lessons 1 to 3, then the phrases for each stageAbout 1 hour
2 to 6One full case, a review and a ten-minute drillAbout 70 minutes
7Read your case-log fixes, rehearse two fit stories, restAbout 1 hour

If you set your interview date on PrepForCase, your home page shows which step of this plan you are on.

Day 1: learn the shape of a case

Do the first three lessons of the course, about 27 minutes in total: how case interviews work, the opening and structuring. Then read the phrases for each stage once, out loud. You now know what the interviewer is scoring and what to say at each step.

If you have another hour, do a first case tonight and treat it as a baseline. If not, your Day 2 case is the baseline. Either way, the goal of that first case is diagnosis, not performance: which two of the six scored skills (clarify and recap, structure, maths and charts, leading, recommendation, communication) went worst?

Days 2 to 6: one case and one drill a day

Each day follows the same pattern:

  1. Read yesterday's fix (2 minutes). One line from your case log, such as "state the next step after every answer".
  2. One full case (35 minutes). With a friend if you can; alone if not. Every case in the casebook has an interviewer script a friend can read from.
  3. Review (10 minutes). Score the six skills, then write the single fix for tomorrow.
  4. One drill (10 minutes). Aimed at your weakest skill. See the sprints below.
  5. Fit (15 minutes, from Day 4). Draft and rehearse one story.

Which cases to choose

Five cases should cover the shapes you are most likely to meet. A sensible spread is a profitability case, a market entry case, an investment or acquisition case, a pricing or growth case and one case that includes a market sizing. Use which framework fits each case type for a quick refresher the night before each.

What a good review looks like

Suppose on Day 3 you found the answer but the interviewer had to prompt you twice to move on. A useless fix is "drive more". A useful one is "after every calculation, say what it means and what I want to look at next". Tomorrow's case is a test of that one fix. Doing five cases in a row while repeating the same error teaches you the error.

Focused sprints for your weakest skill

Days 2 to 6 are five days, which is exactly the length of these sprints. Pick the one or two that match your baseline.

Weak skillSprint over five daysTool
Structure and hypothesis30 structures, six a day: two minutes each, then compare with the modelStructuring drill
Maths and charts30 chart reads (six a day, 90 seconds each) plus ten minutes of speed mathsChart drill, maths drill
RecommendationTen recorded 60-second closes, two a day; count filler words, re-record answer-firstYour phone
Clarify and recap20 case openings, four a day: recap plus three questions onlyA partner, or a case prompt read aloud
Case leadershipFive cases where you announce the next step after every answer; your partner tallies each time you waitA partner
CommunicationDaily voice exercises plus one recorded full caseSpeaking exercises

Fit stories in a week

A strong case cannot make up for a fit answer you cannot explain under follow-up questions. In one week, aim for four stories rather than eight: a leadership story, a time you overcame a setback or failure, a time you persuaded someone, and your proudest achievement. Together they cover most common questions. Add a clear answer to "why consulting, and why this firm?"

Use the fit interview guide to shape each story. Write bullet points, not a script, and tell each one out loud in about two minutes. Then ask yourself the follow-ups an interviewer would: what exactly did you do, what would you do differently, what happened next?

Day 7: review, rehearse, rest

  • Read your case-log fixes from the week. These five or six lines are your briefing notes.
  • Rehearse two fit stories out loud, the two you think you will most likely need.
  • Do one short, familiar exercise so your last practice is a success: a structure you know well or a few quick sums.
  • Prepare logistics. For a video interview, test your camera, microphone and connection, and have paper and pens ready. For an in-person interview, plan the journey and arrive early.
  • Rest. Sleep does more for your performance tomorrow than another case tonight.

On the morning itself, use the 30-minute warm-up.

Mistakes in the final week

  • Cramming new frameworks. You will not use them well under pressure. Stick to the core shapes.
  • Doing three cases a day. Quality of review matters more than volume. One reviewed case beats three unreviewed ones.
  • Ignoring fit until Day 6. Stories need time to find and rehearse. Start them by Day 4 at the latest.
  • Practising only what you are good at. It feels better, and changes nothing.

If you fall behind

You will miss a session. Everyone does. Do not try to catch up by doubling the next day; pick up where the plan is today. If you lose a whole day, drop one full case, not the review or the fit practice.

Check yourself

1. Your baseline case went badly on structure and recommendation, but your maths was fine. How do you use your ten daily drill minutes?

Show the answer

Split them: six two-minute structures from the structuring drill on most days, and two recorded 60-second recommendations. Leave maths alone apart from the calculations inside your daily case.

2. It is the night before. You have done five cases. Should you do a sixth?

Show the answer

No. Read your fixes, rehearse two stories, check logistics and sleep. A sixth case the night before mostly adds anxiety.

3. Write a useful case-log fix for this problem: "I went quiet during the maths."

Show the answer

"Before calculating, say the formula out loud, then say each step as I write it." It is specific, and you can check tomorrow whether you did it.

Where to go next

Start Day 1 now with lesson 1. If your interview turns out to be further away, switch to the three-week plan.
outro: Set your interview date on PrepForCase and your home page will show which step of the plan you are on. Next in this topic: How should you prepare for a case interview in three weeks?
